source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: Builds an open knowledge graph from passages with an LLM, then runs Personalized PageRank (a spreading-activation analogue) from query entities. Beats dense retrievers on two of three multi-hop sets in one step.
numbers: Single-step recall@2/@5, ColBERTv2 vs HippoRAG(ColBERTv2): MuSiQue 37.9/49.2 vs 40.9/51.9; 2Wiki 59.2/68.2 vs 70.7/89.1; HotpotQA 64.7/79.3 vs 60.5/77.7. Average R@5 65.6 vs 72.9. 1,000 questions per set. GPT-3.5-turbo for indexing.
limits: HotpotQA is slightly worse than ColBERTv2. Two hyperparameters tuned on 100 MuSiQue train items. 2Wiki is entity-centric, which favours a graph.
agent_relevance: S3 grounded retrieval: spreading from query entities over a graph beats plain similarity search where evidence is spread across documents, but not where one passage is enough.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: The spreading step itself carries the gain. Using query nodes plus their direct neighbours without PPR is worse than query nodes alone.
numbers: Authors' text: PPR is much more effective than both simple baselines on all three datasets. Ablations (avg R@2/R@5): without node specificity 54.4/67.8; without synonymy edges 57.1/72.5 (2Wiki R@5 89.1 to 85.3); full 57.4/72.9. Damping factor 0.5, synonymy threshold 0.8.
quote: adding the neighborhood of Rq nodes without PPR leads to worse performance than only using the query nodes themselves
limits: The exact numbers for the PPR-replacement rows were garbled in text extraction and are not quoted. Direction is from the paper text.
agent_relevance: Unconstrained neighbour expansion hurts. Weighted, damped propagation is what helps. Do not add naive related neighbours to context.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: Strongest gains are on all-evidence-found: graph spreading finds complete evidence sets that similarity search misses.
numbers: All-recall AR@5, ColBERTv2 vs HippoRAG: MuSiQue 16.1 vs 22.4; 2Wiki 37.1 vs 75.7; HotpotQA 59.0 vs 57.9. Average 37.4 vs 52.0. (Row pairing read from layout.) IRCoT plus HippoRAG avg R@5 77.4 to 78.2 vs IRCoT plus ColBERTv2 70.0.
limits: Same 1,000-question dev sets. HotpotQA is a wash.
agent_relevance: Measure whether all supporting items were found, not average recall. That is what a reasoning step needs.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs
finding: Online cost is far lower than iterative LLM retrieval, and the two methods combine.
numbers: Authors report 10 to 30 times cheaper and 6 to 13 times faster than IRCoT online. QA F1 gains over ColBERTv2 with same reader: up to 3 points MuSiQue, 17 points 2Wiki, 1 point HotpotQA. Indexing costs about 10 times more than IRCoT.
limits: Offline OpenIE with an LLM is the expensive part. Swapping to REBEL for graph building gave large drops.
agent_relevance: One graph build, many cheap multi-hop retrievals. Fits an agent that queries memory many times per task.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2)
finding: First-generation graph retrieval hurt simple factual QA. HippoRAG 2 adds passage nodes and query-to-triple linking and fixes this.
numbers: QA F1 averages, Llama-3.3-70B reader, six RAG sets plus NarrativeQA: NV-Embed-v2 57.0; HippoRAG v1 53.1; HippoRAG 2 59.8; GraphRAG 49.6; RAPTOR 48.8; LightRAG 6.6. Abstract: 7% gain on associative tasks over the best embedding model.
quote: their performance on more basic factual memory tasks drops considerably below standard RAG
limits: Table columns were garbled in extraction. Averages read from the Avg column and consistent with the abstract. Baseline is a 7B embedding model, so gains depend on baseline strength.
agent_relevance: Pure graph spreading loses on single-fact lookups. Use a hybrid of dense match plus spread for S3.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2025) From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs (HippoRAG 2)
finding: Ablations: passage nodes and how the query seeds the graph matter much more than the reset weight.
numbers: Passage recall@5 avg over MuSiQue/2Wiki/HotpotQA: NER-to-node 87.1; query-to-node 74.6; without passage nodes 59.6; without triple filter 81.0. Passage-node weight 0.01 to 0.5: MuSiQue recall 79.9, 80.5, 79.8, 78.4, 77.9.
limits: Row for the full model garbled. The roughly 27 point drop without passage nodes is the clear signal. Recall@5 only.
agent_relevance: Which nodes receive the initial energy is the sensitive step. Spend design effort on seeding, not on tuning decay.

source: Pavlovic, Krasz, Hajdu (2025) Leveraging Spreading Activation for Improved Document Retrieval in KG-Based RAG (SA-RAG)
finding: Classic spreading activation (weighted edges, thresholds a=0.5, d=0.45, r=0.5) over an automatically built heterogeneous knowledge graph, with no LLM-guided graph walk. Works as a plug-in for iterative pipelines.
numbers: 100 random questions per set, phi4 reader. MuSiQue correctness: Naive RAG 46; CoT RAG 56; HippoRAG 2 70; SA-RAG 67; SA-RAG+CoT 75. 2Wiki correctness: Naive 48; CoT 68; HippoRAG 2 76; SA-RAG 76; SA-RAG+CoT 87. Abstract: up to 39 points absolute over naive RAG.
limits: Only 100 questions per benchmark. With gemma3, HippoRAG 2 beat SA-RAG alone on both sets (MuSiQue 59 vs 56; 2Wiki 75 vs 66). Correctness was a manual check. Thresholds set by hand.
agent_relevance: Spreading activation is a cheap, training-free retrieval layer that stacks with chain-of-thought retrieval. Gains depend on the reader's reasoning too.

source: Pavlovic, Krasz, Hajdu (2025) Leveraging Spreading Activation for Improved Document Retrieval in KG-Based RAG (SA-RAG)
finding: Review of the IR lineage: unconstrained spreading activation converges to a fixed state nearly independent of the query, so hop limits, fan-out limits, thresholds and decay below one are required.
numbers: Reported secondhand: early IR work kept only a few hops with decay below one; a later analysis showed pure spread with no limits gives near query-independent results.
limits: Summary of cited papers (Crestani-type work), not opened here. Treat as a pointer.
agent_relevance: Hard guardrail for any activation-spread step: cap hops (Synapse uses 3), set decay and threshold, and re-rank against the query.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Agent memory graph with spreading activation, temporal decay, a fan-effect dilution of hub nodes and lateral inhibition, scored on LoCoMo (GPT-4o-mini). Best average F1 among the memory systems compared.
numbers: Weighted F1 excluding adversarial: SYNAPSE 40.5; Zep 39.7; AriGraph 33.7; A-Mem 33.3; MemGPT 28.0. Multi-hop 35.7 vs A-Mem 27.0; temporal 50.1 vs 45.9; adversarial 96.6 vs Zep 65.4. T=3 steps, retention 0.5, temporal decay 0.01; paired t-test p<0.05, N=500.
limits: Authors' own system and re-runs. Gain over Zep is small (0.8 F1). Authors note sparse early conversations gain little from the graph.
agent_relevance: Direct use of Collins-and-Loftus style spread inside an LLM agent's memory loop, with human-memory phenomena (fan effect, decay) as explicit components.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Ablation: each human-memory mechanism fixes a different failure. No decay wrecks temporal questions. No fan effect floods hub nodes. No lateral inhibition lets hallucination candidates through.
numbers: F1 full vs removed: temporal 50.1 to 14.2 without decay; open-domain 25.9 to 16.8 without fan effect; adversarial 96.6 to 71.5 without lateral inhibition and 67.2 without uncertainty gating; average 40.5 to 30.5 without activation dynamics (static graph), 32.9 with no graph, 25.2 vectors only.
limits: Single benchmark and backbone. Authors admit lateral inhibition can cause cognitive tunneling on simple queries that need exhaustive retrieval.
agent_relevance: Spreading needs three companions: decay for recency, fan-out dilution for hubs, and competition to prune. A static graph scored 30.5, near vectors-only.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) HeLa-Mem: Hebbian Learning and Associative Memory for LLM Agents
finding: Episodic graph whose edges strengthen by co-activation (Hebbian), spreading retrieval along learned edges, and a distilled semantic store. Tested on LoCoMo with four backbones.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini F1: multi-hop 40.14 vs MemoryOS 38.39 vs A-Mem 27.02; temporal 47.29; open domain 29.70; single-hop 51.89. Average 34.74 full vs 32.19 without spreading (multi-hop 36.04 to 33.88). About 1,010 context tokens vs 2,000 to 17,000 for others. Edge decay 0.995, spreading strength 0.1, threshold 0.4.
limits: Removing forgetting made almost no difference on LoCoMo (conversations too short). Authors' own system, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Spreading adds about 2.5 F1 points over dense retrieval here, mostly multi-hop. Learning edge weights from use is a cheap way to get association strength.

source: Misra, Ettinger, Rayz (2020) Exploring BERT's Sensitivity to Lexical Cues using Tests from Semantic Priming
finding: BERT shows semantic priming: a related prime word raises the target's probability versus an unrelated prime. The effect is strongest when the sentence context says little.
numbers: Semantic Priming Project stimuli: 3,058 target-related-unrelated triples (92% of total), 2,112 after filtering (69%). Facilitation falls as context constraint rises (p<.001, BERT-base and BERT-large, mixed-effects model). Two constraint measures correlate -0.89.
quote: The effect decreases as the amount of information provided by the context increases.
limits: Cloze task, not lexical decision. Surprisal stands in for reaction time. BERT only. No chat-tuned model tested.
agent_relevance: Cheap associations help most when the prompt is vague. When context already constrains the answer, a related word adds little.

source: Misra, Ettinger, Rayz (2020) Exploring BERT's Sensitivity to Lexical Cues using Tests from Semantic Priming
finding: In highly constrained contexts a related word can distract BERT, lowering the target's probability below the no-prime baseline (mispriming).
numbers: Strict criterion (facilitation positive and P(T|R,C)>P(T|C)): from the 8th constraint bin BERT-base is primed in 49% or fewer cases (word-prime setting). Larger facilitation for synonym (418 pairs), category (164), antonym (153) than for other relations (phrasal associate 263 and 151, script 124, perceptual 90, functional 73, instrument 35).
limits: Pair counts differ by relation, so relation comparisons are rough. Distraction examples are qualitative.
agent_relevance: A related-but-wrong retrieved item can lower the right answer's odds. Retrieval should be filtered, not just broadened.

source: Abramski et al. (2024) The LLM World of Words English free association norms generated by large language models
finding: Three LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Claude Haiku) gave free associations to the same 12,282 cues as the human Small World of Words, 100 response sets per cue, over 3 million responses. Spreading activation on the resulting networks reproduces human priming data.
numbers: spreadr on 50 prime-target pairs (Semantic Priming Project): Wilcoxon effect size related vs unrelated 0.870 humans, 0.859 Mistral, 0.869 Llama3, 0.866 Haiku (all p<.001). Spearman of activation vs reaction time: -0.626 humans, -0.615 Mistral, -0.614 Llama3, -0.662 Haiku.
limits: Only 50 pairs and one task. Validity shown by simulation on the network, not by LLM behaviour in a priming task. Responses are sampled repeatedly.
agent_relevance: LLM-generated association networks can stand in for human ones to rank prime-target strength.

source: Abramski, Rossetti, Stella (2026) The role of System 1 and System 2 semantic memory structure in human and LLM biases
finding: Three-layer semantic networks (free associations, definitions, categorical relations) from humans, Mistral and Llama3, with spreading activation used to measure gender bias. Human bias is highest in the associative layer and falls in definitional and categorical layers. LLMs show no consistent drop.
numbers: Humans: stereotype effect sizes decrease from associative to definitional and categorical layers across all four topics (traits, professions, home/career, arts/sciences). Mistral and Llama3: layer pattern varies by topic and sign flips (Llama3 definitions layer male-consistent for traits and arts/sciences, inconsistent for professions and home/career). Layers stay irreducible only in humans.
quote: semantic memory structures are irreducible only in humans
limits: Two open models only. Effect sizes are in figures; no table values read. One bias dimension (gender). Dual-process framing is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Associative links carry bias; structured links dampen it in people but apparently not in LLMs. Do not expect structured retrieval alone to remove model bias.

source: Kinney (2025) LLM-Generated Semantic Networks Predict Semantic Priming Effects on Human Reaction Times in a Word-Recognition Task
finding: Gemini was prompted to output a semantic graph (JSON triples) linking all words of the Hutchison et al. (2013) priming data. Shortest path length between prime and target predicts human reaction time in every graph tested.
numbers: 4,988 triple lists over temperatures 0, .3, .7, 1 and several max-output-token settings, two Gemini 1.5 versions (flash, pro), 32 mixed-effects models. Best graph (flash, temp .3, 1024 tokens): path-length beta = .044, p<.001. Worst (pro, temp 0, 1536 tokens): beta = .031, p<.001. Max shortest path differs between models, t = 21.75, p = 9.3e-13.
limits: Two models, one dataset, short paper. The smaller, more hallucination-prone model gave denser and better-predicting graphs. No comparison to human association networks.
agent_relevance: LLM-built graphs are usable for spread-based relatedness. Denser graphs predicted humans better, a warning against over-pruning a memory graph.

source: Meghdadi, Duff, Demberg (2026) Integrating language model embeddings into the ACT-R cognitive modeling framework
finding: Replaces ACT-R's hand-coded association strengths with Word2Vec or BERT cosine similarity to drive spreading activation, and predicts item-level lexical-decision times in the Semantic Priming Project.
numbers: Spearman rho with RT: EMMA-only 0.30; frequency-only ACT-R 0.42; ACT-R with word length 0.48; embedding spreading M2a Word2Vec 0.50, M2b BERT 0.49; with approximate fan effect M3a 0.51, M3b 0.50. Plain linear regression (log frequency, cosine similarity, length) 0.51 (CI .49 to .52). M3a vs M2a Williams T2 = 2.39, p = .02.
limits: The spreading model matches but does not beat a simple regression on the same predictors. Gain of spreading over frequency-and-length baseline is about 0.02 rho. Frequency-only model is 0.42 in the table but 0.41 in the paper text. Latent factors beyond similarity remain.
agent_relevance: Embedding cosine already captures most of what spreading adds for single-pair priming. Spreading's edge shows in multi-hop chains, not pairwise relatedness.

source: Han et al. (2025) RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights
finding: Independent test: graph retrieval is not uniformly better. Plain RAG wins single-hop. The best graph methods edge ahead on multi-hop. Naive knowledge-graph variants lose badly.
numbers: NQ F1: RAG 64.78; HippoRAG2 61.03; Community-GraphRAG local 63.01; KG-GraphRAG triplets only 34.28. HotpotQA F1: RAG 60.04; HippoRAG2 63.01. MultiHop-RAG overall: RAG 67.02; HippoRAG2 70.27; Community local 69.01; triplets-only KG 41.24. Temporal queries RAG 30.70 vs HippoRAG2 49.91; null queries RAG 96.01 vs HippoRAG2 85.71.
limits: Graphs built with GPT-4o-mini; outcomes vary with design choices. HippoRAG2 hurts on null and single-hop queries.
agent_relevance: Tempers HippoRAG claims: about +3 F1 on multi-hop, a loss on single-hop. Route by question type or use both retrievers.

source: Han et al. (2025) RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights
finding: Reranking and iterative retrieval (IRCoT) improve every method over vanilla inference, so spreading is one layer among several.
numbers: Reported in Figure 1 for NQ and MultiHop-RAG: improvement for all methods. Exact values not read from the figure.
limits: Figure-only numbers.
agent_relevance: Test spreading on top of the existing retrieval loop, not against it.

source: Collins and Loftus (1975) A spreading-activation theory of semantic processing
finding: The founding theory: concepts are nodes, links vary in strength, activation spreads in parallel and fades with distance; relatedness is found where spread from two concepts meets. Cited by every machine paper above as the root.
numbers: Not extracted this session. See evidence_a and evidence_b for human data.
limits: Not opened in this angle; known here only through its citation in Abramski 2024, Pavlovic 2025 and Kinney 2025.
agent_relevance: Gives the design vocabulary: link strength, decay, intersection search.

source: Crestani (1997) Application of spreading activation techniques in information retrieval
finding: Classic IR survey of constrained spreading activation over term-document networks as a complement to standard search. Described in Pavlovic 2025.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Secondhand only. Check the title and DOI before relying on them.
agent_relevance: Older precedent that spread works only when constrained.

source: Synthesis across SYNAPSE, HeLa-Mem, SA-RAG, HippoRAG, HippoRAG 2 (all opened)
finding: Across five 2024-2026 systems the recipe is the same: embed for seeds, spread 2 to 3 hops with decay, combine with the dense score, let a language model read the result. Gains over dense retrieval are largest on multi-hop and temporal questions.
numbers: Settings: Synapse T=3, retention 0.5; SA-RAG decay 0.45, threshold 0.5; HippoRAG damping 0.5; HeLa-Mem strength 0.1, threshold 0.4. Multi-hop gains: HippoRAG 2Wiki R@5 +20.9 over ColBERTv2; Synapse multi-hop F1 +8.7 over A-Mem; HeLa-Mem spreading ablation multi-hop +2.2.
limits: Each paper is by its own authors on Wikipedia QA or LoCoMo. No head-to-head of all five on one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Defaults for S3 retrieval: 2 to 3 hops, decay about 0.5, threshold gate, hybrid score.

source: Synthesis: what the machines do not reproduce
finding: The human pattern that associative links drive automatic priming while structured knowledge restrains bias was not reproduced in LLMs. BERT priming does fade under context constraint, a loose analogue of human context effects.
numbers: Abramski 2026: no consistent layer pattern in Mistral or Llama3. Misra 2020: facilitation falls with constraint, p<.001.
limits: No study found testing chat-tuned LLMs on classic in-context priming (lexical decision style). That is a gap, not a null result.
agent_relevance: Do not assume an LLM primed by retrieved text behaves like a human. Test it. Padding with related words can mislead.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Spreading activation keeps working when the query shares few words with the memory. On LoCoMo subsets chosen for low query-memory similarity, SYNAPSE barely drops while a dense-embedding agent memory collapses.
numbers: Relative F1 drop on low-similarity subsets: SYNAPSE 5.3% (threshold 0.5) and 7.4% (threshold 0.3); A-Mem 43.1% and 56.3%. SYNAPSE adversarial F1 95.3 and 93.7 there; A-Mem multi-hop 20.2 vs SYNAPSE 42.8.
limits: Authors' own subset construction; single benchmark; GPT-4o-mini family.
agent_relevance: Spread recovers items that similarity search cannot reach. That is the core promise for S3 when the question is phrased unlike the stored note.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SYNAPSE: Empowering LLM Agents with Episodic-Semantic Memory via Spreading Activation
finding: Efficiency: the activated subgraph is small, so cost and context fall while accuracy rises.
numbers: Per query: SYNAPSE 814 tokens, 1.9 s, $0.24 per 1k queries, F1 40.5; full-context LoCoMo baseline 16,910 tokens, 8.2 s, $2.67, F1 25.6; A-Mem 2,520 tokens, 5.4 s, $0.50, F1 33.3; LangMem 717 tokens, 0.6 s, F1 34.3. Sensitivity: best at propagation depth T=3, inhibition top-M about 7, top-k about 30.
limits: Latency on one A100 averaged over 100 queries; authors' own measurement. LangMem is faster and cheaper per query.
agent_relevance: Retrieving a small activated subgraph beats stuffing the full history; cap depth and top-k.
